children: , the integrated-energy giant and one of the world's biggest LNG traders, estimated that Middle East shipping disruptions wiped roughly 36 million tons of LNG from the market in 2026, according to Reuters. Its U.S. shares fell approximately 2.5% to $96.49, based on the latest quoted price.

The disruption sent Asian spot LNG prices from roughly $10 to nearly $30 per million British thermal units, forcing some buyers in China, India and Pakistan to pull back consumption or turn toward coal and oil. That price shock cuts both ways for Shell: scarcity can create lucrative trading opportunities, but LNG near $30 becomes too expensive for many price-sensitive customers. Industry executives expect demand to strengthen again if incoming supply eventually drags prices toward the $7-to-$9 range.

Shell sold 19.2 million tons of LNG in the second quarter while producing 7.9 million tons itself, putting its sales volume at roughly 2.4 times its own liquefaction output. That gap highlights the power of Shell's global trading portfolio: it can source cargoes beyond its own plants and redirect molecules toward the markets willing to pay most. The valuation picture adds another wrinklethe shares at $96.49 sit 16.48% above the $82.84 GF Value, suggesting investors are already paying a meaningful premium to GuruFocus' estimate of fair value.

title: Shell Falls 2.5% as 36 Million Missing Tons Reprice LNG Demand
